<div class="honest">
<p>NVIDIA Warp is an excellent per-thread kernel compiler: it is the fastest arm in 2 of the 12 RK4 cells this card runs, and when every sample runs all 1000 steps it ties eagle.simulate: 1.71 ms against eagle.simulate's 1.75 ms.</p>
<p>On memory, hawk + eagle's lower-level building blocks go lighter than Warp: 1.2× the minimum against Warp's 1.8×. eagle.simulate keeps room to compact the batch and uses 1.1×.</p>
<p class="fine">Measured on NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3. <a href="https://amasat01.github.io/eagle/content/performance.html">Every number, every arm</a>.</p>
</div>

<div class="honest">
<p>NVIDIA Warp is an excellent per-thread kernel compiler: when every sample runs all 1000 steps eagle.simulate beats it: 103 ms against Warp's 119 ms.</p>
<p>On memory, hawk + eagle's lower-level building blocks go lighter than Warp: 1.1× the minimum against Warp's 1.8×. eagle.simulate keeps room to compact the batch and uses 1.1×.</p>
<p class="fine">Measured on NVIDIA L4. <a href="https://amasat01.github.io/eagle/content/performance.html">Every number, every arm</a>.</p>
</div>

<div class="honest">
<p>NVIDIA Warp is an excellent per-thread kernel compiler: it is the fastest arm in 1 of the 12 RK4 cells this card runs, and when every sample runs all 1000 steps eagle.simulate beats it: 4.85 ms against Warp's 6.67 ms.</p>
<p>On memory, hawk + eagle's lower-level building blocks go lighter than Warp: 1.1× the minimum against Warp's 1.8×. eagle.simulate keeps room to compact the batch and uses 1.1×.</p>
<p class="fine">Measured on NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB. <a href="https://amasat01.github.io/eagle/content/performance.html">Every number, every arm</a>.</p>
</div>
</section>

<div class="honest">
<p>NVIDIA Warp is an excellent per-thread kernel compiler: when every sample runs all 1000 steps eagle.simulate beats it: 191 ms against Warp's 220 ms.</p>
<p>On memory, hawk + eagle's lower-level building blocks go lighter than Warp: 1.1× the minimum against Warp's 1.8×. eagle.simulate keeps room to compact the batch and uses 1.1×.</p>
<p class="fine">Measured on Tesla T4. <a href="https://amasat01.github.io/eagle/content/performance.html">Every number, every arm</a>.</p>
</div>
</section>

<div class="honest">
<p>NVIDIA Warp is an excellent per-thread kernel compiler: when every sample runs all 1000 steps eagle.simulate beats it: 640 ms against Warp's 699 ms.</p>
<p>On memory, hawk + eagle's lower-level building blocks go lighter than Warp: 1.1× the minimum against Warp's 1.8×. eagle.simulate keeps room to compact the batch and uses 1.1×.</p>
<p class="fine">Measured on Quadro P2000. <a href="https://amasat01.github.io/eagle/content/performance.html">Every number, every arm</a>.</p>
</div>

<div class="honest">
<p>NVIDIA Warp is an excellent per-thread kernel compiler: when every sample runs all 1000 steps eagle.simulate beats it: 27.6 ms against Warp's 32.1 ms.</p>
<p>On memory, hawk + eagle's lower-level building blocks go lighter than Warp: 1.2× the minimum against Warp's 1.8×. eagle.simulate keeps room to compact the batch and uses 1.1×.</p>
<p class="fine">Measured on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition. <a href="https://amasat01.github.io/eagle/content/performance.html">Every number, every arm</a>.</p>
</div>

<p class="axis-note worlds-note">Columns: Simulation on the left, AI on the right, blending where they meet. Rows: the CPU on top, the GPU below. A tool's shape encloses the blocks its own documentation shows a designed feature or API for, and never a block it does not; a workaround (masking every lane, raw CUDA strings, running the slowest sample to the end) does not count. Every covered cell links to its source in the table. The tools are complementary; overlap is not a ranking.</p>

<dl class="radar-defs" aria-label="What each axis measures"><dt>Ensemble speed</dt><dd>How fast a batch of independent samples runs: uneven, regular, small and adaptive workloads.</dd><dt>Footprint and turnaround</dt><dd>What the work costs around the run: the memory it holds, the time to compile and the code to write.</dd><dt>Tensors and precision (qualitative)</dt><dd>Dense tensor maths, array-style code and half precision: where PyTorch and JAX lead.</dd><dt>One-sample authoring (qualitative)</dt><dd>Writing the code for one sample and getting derivatives of it.</dd><dt>Low-level control (qualitative)</dt><dd>How much of the execution you control from the tool&#x27;s own language.</dd><dt>Reach (qualitative)</dt><dd>Where the tool fits in: your arrays, deployment outside Python and extension to new targets.</dd></dl>

<p class="axis-note radar-note radar-note-lead">Every measured axis is the per-sample ensemble workload raptor is built for; dense tensor maths, training and half precision are the qualitative axes, where PyTorch and JAX lead. Outer is better; overlaps are complementary, not a ranking.</p>
<p class="axis-note radar-note radar-caption-control">NVIDIA Warp gives you near-total control of every kernel, short of raw CUDA. raptor hands that control to the engine on purpose, so compaction and the launch shape are decided at run time; the two are different trade-offs, not a ranking.</p>
<details class="radar-data radar-howto"><summary>How to read this radar</summary><p class="axis-note radar-note">Each of the six majors is the plain mean of its minor axes (the detailed radar draws every minor), with equal weights and the same rule for every tool; a minor a tool has no reading on is left out of its mean and the major's marker is drawn hollow. Hover or tap a major to see its minors.</p><ul class="radar-howto-list radar-howto-majors"><li><strong>Ensemble speed</strong>: Uneven ensembles, Regular ensembles, Small jobs and Adaptive ODEs; measured.</li><li><strong>Footprint and turnaround</strong>: Memory, Compile time and Code size; measured.</li><li><strong>Tensors and precision</strong>: Tensor workloads, Array-style programming and Half precision and below; qualitative.</li><li><strong>One-sample authoring</strong>: Single-thread abstraction and Differentiable kernels; qualitative.</li><li><strong>Low-level control</strong>: A single axis, so nothing is averaged; qualitative.</li><li><strong>Reach</strong>: Works with your arrays, Deploy outside Python and Extensibility; qualitative.</li></ul><p class="axis-note radar-note">Each measured axis is stretched over its own best-to-worst range, so ring labels differ per axis (compile time: fixed, 0.1 s to 100 s; code size: at least 4x). Axes are grouped by theme, so read the axes, not the area.</p><p class="axis-note radar-note">Italic axes are the author's judgement, not measurements: hollow markers, a linear scale, and no marker where a tool has no reading. A hollow marker on a measured axis means a minor is missing or, for compile time, is the tool's simple-kernel time. The hover panel has each axis's full wording.</p><p class="axis-note radar-note"><a href="https://amasat01.github.io/eagle/content/performance.html">Every number, in the full tables</a>.</p></details>

<p class="axis-note worlds-note">Columns: Simulation on the left, AI on the right, blending where they meet. Rows: the CPU on top, the GPU below. A tool's shape encloses the blocks its own documentation shows a designed feature or API for, and never a block it does not; a workaround (masking every lane, raw CUDA strings, running the slowest sample to the end) does not count. Every covered cell links to its source in the table. The tools are complementary; overlap is not a ranking.</p>

<dl class="radar-defs" aria-label="What each axis measures"><dt>Ensemble speed</dt><dd>How fast a batch of independent samples runs: uneven, regular, small and adaptive workloads.</dd><dt>Footprint and turnaround</dt><dd>What the work costs around the run: the memory it holds, the time to compile and the code to write.</dd><dt>Tensors and precision (qualitative)</dt><dd>Dense tensor maths, array-style code and half precision: where PyTorch and JAX lead.</dd><dt>One-sample authoring (qualitative)</dt><dd>Writing the code for one sample and getting derivatives of it.</dd><dt>Low-level control (qualitative)</dt><dd>How much of the execution you control from the tool&#x27;s own language.</dd><dt>Reach (qualitative)</dt><dd>Where the tool fits in: your arrays, deployment outside Python and extension to new targets.</dd></dl>

<p class="axis-note radar-note radar-note-lead">Every measured axis is the per-sample ensemble workload raptor is built for; dense tensor maths, training and half precision are the qualitative axes, where PyTorch and JAX lead. Outer is better; overlaps are complementary, not a ranking.</p>
<p class="axis-note radar-note radar-caption-control">NVIDIA Warp gives you near-total control of every kernel, short of raw CUDA. raptor hands that control to the engine on purpose, so compaction and the launch shape are decided at run time; the two are different trade-offs, not a ranking.</p>
<details class="radar-data radar-howto"><summary>How to read this radar</summary><p class="axis-note radar-note">Each of the six majors is the plain mean of its minor axes (the detailed radar draws every minor), with equal weights and the same rule for every tool; a minor a tool has no reading on is left out of its mean and the major's marker is drawn hollow. Hover or tap a major to see its minors.</p><ul class="radar-howto-list radar-howto-majors"><li><strong>Ensemble speed</strong>: Uneven ensembles, Regular ensembles, Small jobs and Adaptive ODEs; measured.</li><li><strong>Footprint and turnaround</strong>: Memory, Compile time and Code size; measured.</li><li><strong>Tensors and precision</strong>: Tensor workloads, Array-style programming and Half precision and below; qualitative.</li><li><strong>One-sample authoring</strong>: Single-thread abstraction and Differentiable kernels; qualitative.</li><li><strong>Low-level control</strong>: A single axis, so nothing is averaged; qualitative.</li><li><strong>Reach</strong>: Works with your arrays, Deploy outside Python and Extensibility; qualitative.</li></ul><p class="axis-note radar-note">Each measured axis is stretched over its own best-to-worst range, so ring labels differ per axis (compile time: fixed, 0.1 s to 100 s; code size: at least 4x). Axes are grouped by theme, so read the axes, not the area.</p><p class="axis-note radar-note">Italic axes are the author's judgement, not measurements: hollow markers, a linear scale, and no marker where a tool has no reading. A hollow marker on a measured axis means a minor is missing or, for compile time, is the tool's simple-kernel time. The hover panel has each axis's full wording.</p><p class="axis-note radar-note"><a href="https://amasat01.github.io/eagle/content/performance.html">Every number, in the full tables</a>.</p></details>
